questions.question: What is implicit interface satisfaction in Go?
questions.title: Implicit Satisfaction
questions.direct_answer: No 'implements' keyword — a type satisfies an interface by HAVING the methods. The check is structural: if File has Read() string, it satisfies interface{ Read() string }.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of the compile-time check: interface satisfaction is decidable from method signatures alone. The compiler builds each named type's method set (name + signature pairs); an assignment var r Reader = x compiles iff Reader's method list is a subset of method-set(x). The failure error is precise: the missing method name(s), verbatim — 'File does not implement Reader (missing Read method)' — the diagnostic that teaches the rule.

What the check can't see, and why interface{} is different: an empty interface requires zero methods — every type satisfies it vacuously. That's why interface{} holds anything: the structural check on an empty set passes universally. It's also why interface{} carries no information about what the value can do. (Go 1.18's 'any' is a synonym — same semantics, shorter spelling.)

The duck-typing comparison and its precise boundary: Go is NOT runtime duck typing (Python — method presence checked at call time, failure at runtime). Go's check is compile-time and structural — full signature match, not just name match (a Read() int does not satisfy Read() string). The accurate framing: structural typing with static verification — the ergonomics of duck typing, the safety of a checked implements clause.

The design consequence for API authors: accept interfaces, return concrete types. The consumer can always narrow a concrete return to whatever interface they need; a producer accepting a concrete type forces the consumer to construct it. Accepting the interface (usually one method) lets callers pass anything that fits — the flexibility flows to the boundary where the requirements live.

questions.question: Can a type satisfy an interface without knowing the interface exists?
questions.title: When would you use Implicit Satisfaction in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Yes — that's the design's point. Satisfaction is structural: the type has the methods; the interface lists methods; the compiler checks any assignment.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Yes — that's the design's point.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Yes, and it's not an edge case — it's how the standard library itself was largely built:

```go
func (f File) Read() string { return "reading " + f.name }

type Reader interface{ Read() string }

var r Reader = File{"x"}   // the fit is discovered HERE
```

File's author never wrote 'implements Reader'; Reader's author never listed File. The compiler confirms the structural fit at the assignment — the only place the two ever meet.

The historical proof is the io package: many io.Reader implementations predate or independently exist of the interface. Contrast with Java's nominal system: a class not declared 'implements Serializable' cannot be serialized, no matter its structure — the type's author must have planned every interface it will ever satisfy.

The practical upside you use daily: adapting types you don't own. A third-party struct has a Close method — you can define your own Closer interface and accept that struct through it, without touching the vendor code. The interface follows the need, not the type's design.

The discipline that keeps it honest: the compile-time check IS the contract — no runtime verification, no 'close enough' (signature must match exactly, including receiver kinds via the method-set rule).

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The dependency-inversion consequence — the architectural payoff: in nominal systems, the interface is a hub — the type imports the interface's package to declare the relationship. Dependencies radiate FROM implementations TO interface definitions. In Go, the arrow inverts: only the USE site knows the interface. The implementation package has zero references to it.

That inversion enables the pattern the standard library normalizes: define the interface where you USE it, as small as your actual need. A function that only needs to call Read accepts an interface{ Read([]byte) (int, error) }. The producer remains concretely typed and testable; the consumer's requirement is one line; and the interface can CHANGE without breaking the producer — only the use sites compile against it.

The compile-time cost: signature comparison, cached per (interface, type) pair, effectively free. The runtime cost is the itable: the FIRST assignment of a concrete type to an interface builds a method table for that pair (cached globally thereafter) — the method call is a table lookup + indirect call. That's the entire overhead — one indirection, amortized to zero after the first box.

The failure mode the design accepts: accidental satisfaction. A type CAN satisfy an interface its author never intended. In nominal systems, implements is a statement of intent; in Go, intent is inferred from structure alone. The mitigation is cultural: interfaces defined by consumers with exact needs, and for genuinely accidental overlap — explicitness elsewhere (a distinctive method name, a marker method for sealed hierarchies).

questions.question: What is interface embedding, and how does it compose interfaces?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Implicit Satisfaction
questions.direct_answer: Embedding interfaces inside an interface combines their method lists — the composed interface's method set is the union. io.ReadCloser is Reader + Closer.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Embedding interfaces inside an interface combines their method lists — the composed interface's method set is the union.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Admin] --> EMBED[User embedded]
    EMBED --> PF[field: Name promoted]
    EMBED --> PM[method: Greet promoted]
    A --> OWN[field: Level — depth 0]
    PF --> LOOKUP[name lookup: depth 0 first, then depth 1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of the union: the compiler computes an embedded-interface's method set at definition time — the composition is a set of (name, signature) pairs, flattened from the embedded interfaces' own sets (which may themselves be compositions — the flattening is transitive; cycles are a compile error). The result is indistinguishable from having written the methods out: interface{ Reader; Closer } and interface{ Read(); Close() } are the SAME method set — embedding is pure expression, not a new mechanism.

That equivalence has a versioning consequence: if Reader grows a method, every embedded composition grows too — ReadCloser compiled against old-Reader now demands the new method. The io package's stability discipline (Reader and Writer have never changed since Go 1) exists precisely to protect this. When you own the atoms, growing a method in them is a breaking change rippling through every composer.

Embedding a concrete type in an interface is a compile error (interfaces compose interfaces only); embedding an interface in a STRUCT is the delegation pattern — the struct gains the interface's methods as promotion, with the embedded value's implementation behind them. The two embeddings (interface-in-interface for composition, interface-in-struct for delegation) are the twin idioms of Go's interface architecture — same keyword, two orthogonal capabilities, and interviews often probe exactly whether a candidate keeps them separate.

questions.question: How do you check whether a value satisfies an interface at runtime?
questions.title: compare Implicit Satisfaction with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: Type assertion with the comma-ok form: v, ok := x.(Reader) — ok is true when x's dynamic type satisfies Reader. Or a type switch over multiple interfaces.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Type assertion with the comma-ok form: v, ok := x.(Reader) — ok is true when x's dynamic type satisfies Reader.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The comma-ok assertion works for interfaces as well as concrete types:

```go
var x interface{} = File{"b"}

if r, ok := x.(Reader); ok {
    fmt.Println(r.Read())   // runs — File satisfies Reader
}
```

The one-assignment form (r := x.(Reader)) panics on failure — the comma-ok form is the graceful probe.

When the question spans several candidates, the type switch:

```go
switch v := x.(type) {
case Reader:
    fmt.Println("it reads:", v.Read())
case Closer:
    fmt.Println("it closes")
default:
    fmt.Println("neither")
}
```

The first case whose method set the dynamic type satisfies wins, and v is bound to that type inside the case.

Where this pattern lives in real code: error handling (errors.As is the modern form), serialization layers (does it implement MarshalJSON?), optional capability interfaces (io.WriterTo as a fast path). The capability-probe idiom — 'if the value can do X, use the fast path' — is the standard library's own style (fmt checks for Formatter, Stringer, error in order).

The failure mode to know: a typed-nil inside an interface can satisfy the assertion (ok true) and then panic on method call through a nil receiver. ok answers 'does the dynamic TYPE satisfy' — it knows nothing about the VALUE's nilness.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q[the question] --> R[the core rule]
    R --> EX[the small example]
    EX --> B[the boundary — where the rule ends]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The assertion's mechanics: x.(Reader) reads the interface value's type descriptor, checks Reader's method list against that type's itable, and on success produces a NEW interface value (type and data unchanged, reinterpreted as Reader). The ok form branches instead of panicking; the check is the same method-subset comparison the compiler does at assignment — done at runtime because x's dynamic type is a runtime fact.

The type switch compiles to a sequence of assertions with one optimization: it reads x's type descriptor ONCE, then compares against each case's type (concrete cases: pointer comparison; interface cases: itable lookup). The first match binds v — and v's static type per-case is the case's type, so the case body gets a typed value with full method access.

The capability-probe pattern's runtime cost: each probe is a type-descriptor comparison — nanoseconds. That's why fmt's ordered checking (Formatter then Stringer then error) is viable in a formatting hot path: three nearly-free probes choosing the richest behavior present. The pattern generalizes to any layered API: try the specialized interface, fall back to the general one.

The nil-dynamic-value subtlety, closed: ok is a statement about the TYPE fit. The VALUE can be a typed nil — the assertion succeeds, methods dispatch, and a pointer-receiver method that dereferences panics. The complete pattern: assert, THEN nil-check the concrete value — or design methods that tolerate nil receivers.

questions.question: What is the difference between a nil interface and an interface holding a nil pointer?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Implicit Satisfaction
questions.direct_answer: Nil interface: both words zero — == nil is true. Interface holding a nil *T: the type word is set — == nil is FALSE. The classic Go bug: returning a typed nil in an error path.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Nil interface: both words zero — == nil is true. Interface holding a nil *T: the type word is set — == nil is FALSE.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The executed proof:

```go
var g Greeter          // nil interface
g == nil               // true

var p *User            // nil pointer
var g2 Greeter = p     // box the typed nil
g2 == nil              // false!
```

Two states that look identical in casual reading. The interface value is (type, value) — two words. The nil interface has both zero. The typed-nil interface has the type word set (*User) and the value word nil — the interface KNOWS its type, and that makes it non-nil.

Why this is Go's most famous bug: a helper returns (nil, err) — but if the function's return type is an INTERFACE, the caller's err != nil check sees the typed nil and the 'error path' looks like success:

```go
func loadUser() *User { return nil }
var g Greeter = loadUser()
g == nil         // false — the trap sprung
```

The fix patterns: return concrete types from functions (the caller boxes — a nil *User compared as a pointer IS nil); or return the interface type and explicitly return nil (the literal — the nil interface); or use errors instead of nil returns for failure.

The comparison rule in one line: interface == nil compares BOTH words — type AND value must be nil. A typed nil has a non-nil type word, so the comparison fails.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    NILVAR[nil channel] --> SENDS[send: parks forever]
    NILVAR --> RECV[receive: parks forever]
    NILVAR --> SELECT[select: case disabled — the one legal use]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two-word representation explains everything: interface values are (type-descriptor pointer, data pointer). The comparison g == nil compiles to 'both words are zero.' Boxing p (a nil *User) into Greeter writes the type word (*User's descriptor — non-zero) and the data word (the nil pointer, copied into the interface's storage). So the interface is 'a *User that happens to be nil' — a meaningful state, distinct from 'nothing.'

The method-call behavior through a typed nil: calling g.Greet() finds *User's Greet in the itable and passes the nil pointer as the receiver. If Greet is a pointer-receiver method that dereferences — panic. If it handles nil receivers — it works, a legitimate pattern: nil-receiver methods.

The standard library's own incidence — where typed nils are deliberate: a nil *bytes.Buffer, a nil map inside a struct field (methods on nil receivers work: append to nil slices, read from nil maps — the nil-tolerant method family). The bug shape is specifically the INTERFACE boundary: code that would have compared a concrete nil correctly compares a boxed typed nil incorrectly. The rule that prevents it: never return a typed nil where the caller will see an interface — return untyped nil or a concrete type.
